I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

vignette: Mark, a 32-year-old European American combat pilot, has been struggling with profound psychological distress following a traumatic sexual assault. His life and sense of security have been profoundly disrupted since the incident. Mark’s experience of the assault was so intense that even the slightest trigger can plunge him back into a state of acute fear and hypervigilance. The assault occurred in a dimly lit parking lot near his base. He had just finished a late shift when he was ambushed by someone he knew, which made the betrayal feel even more devastating. Since then, any situation that seems unpredictable or where people act suspiciously can send Mark into a state of high alert. Last week, while on a training mission, he woke up from a nightmare and immediately felt as though he needed to be on guard. The dream had been vivid, with dark figures lurking around every corner, mirroring the unpredictability that still haunts him. Mark’s heightened sense of threat is most evident in his home environment. He feels vulnerable even inside his own home and constantly listens for any sounds that might indicate someone is entering. This hypervigilance has led to frequent startling at ordinary sounds like a car door slamming or a phone ringing, which he interprets as potential threats. The more often these triggers activate his sense of threat, the deeper Mark’s negative appraisals about himself and the world have become. Mark feels that his reactions since the event show he is a lousy coper. This belief exacerbates his fear and makes him feel even more vulnerable. He has lost faith in people, life, or any higher power that could protect him from such harm. His sense of betrayal by someone he trusted further reinforces this negative outlook on life and human nature. These negative appraisals, in turn, intensify Mark’s hypervigilance and his triggers. When Mark feels betrayed and believes he is a poor coper, he becomes more likely to perceive any unpredictable situation as threatening. This cycle has created a vicious loop where his fear and hyperalertness are constantly reinforced by the negative thoughts that plague him. The stress of constantly feeling threatened has begun to take a toll on Mark’s work as well. His hypervigilance makes it difficult for him to focus during flights, and he frequently feels anxious about what might happen if someone were to attack him again in the air. This fear has led to several instances where he avoided social situations altogether, exacerbating his sense of isolation. It was a particularly harrowing incident at work that finally prompted Mark to seek help. During a routine flight, he heard an unfamiliar noise and immediately panicked, believing it was someone trying to sabotage him. His intense reaction forced him to land prematurely, and the stress from this event convinced him that he needed professional support to manage his overwhelming fear and distress. Mark’s current state is marked by deep anxiety and a pervasive sense of insecurity. He is most afraid of reliving the trauma and feeling helpless again. What Mark hopes for now is a way to regain control over his life, to feel safe both at work and in everyday situations, and to rebuild his faith in himself and others. His journey toward recovery begins with understanding that he can learn to manage these overwhelming feelings and start rebuilding trust and safety in his world.
